                                                 I.     INTRODUCTION.


                Q.   PLEASE STATE YOUR NAME AND BUSINESS ADDRESS.

                Q.   BY WHOM ARE YOU EMPLOYED AND IN WHAT CAPACITY?

                A.   I am currently self-employed as an independent consultant in matters related to electric
                     transmission systems planning, routing, construction, and operation.

                Q.   ON WHOSE BEHALF ARE YOU TESTIFYING IN THIS PROCEEDING?

                A.   I am testifying on behalf of the Ben E. Keith Company and the Jan Yates Boultinghouse
                     Family Trust, including its trustee Jan Yates Boultinghouse and its successor trustee,
                     Kenna Boultinghouse Squires (together the "Joint Landowners").

                Q.   ARE YOU THE SAME MARK D. ANDERSON THAT TESTIFIED PREVIOUSLY?

                A.   Yes. My prior testimony was filed as Docket 59475, Item 4189.

                Q.   AFTER REVIEWING THE TESTIMONY SUBMITTED BY VARIOUS
                     WITNESSES IN THIS PROCEEDING, DO YOU HAVE ANY GENERAL
                     OBSERVATIONS?

                A.   Yes. In my experience, large transmission routing proceedings commonly involve
                     competing landowner, environmental, operational, recreational, and development concerns
                     throughout the study area. Many intervenors and witnesses they engage understandably
                     focus on the impacts associated with particular properties, links, land uses, or localized
                     areas of concern that directly affect them or the parties they represent. At the same time,
                     the Commission' s routing responsibility requires a broader comparative evaluation of
                     competing routing considerations across the entire corridor, including engineering,
                     constructability, environmental impacts, community impacts, route efficiency, habitable
                     structures, and overall system planning considerations. In my opinion, the Joint Applicants'
                     evaluation reflects that broader corridor-wide balancing process.

                                           II.        REBUTTAL TESTIMONY.

                     A.     JASON HOWTON.

                Q.   HAVE YOU REVIEWED THE TESTIMONY OF MR. JASON HOWTON?




                                      Rebuttal Testimony ofMark D. Anderson at Page 4
  1   A.   Yes. Mr. Howton, a pro se intervenor, states he is a person qualified by professional
 2        experience under Texas Rules ofEvidence 702 to offer expert opinion on "the specific gaps
 3        in the Applicants' cost estimation methodology particularly the omission of current tariff
 4        exposure from their estimates" and on the supply chain risks that he believes renders the
 5        Applicants' estimates to be "materially understated." He focuses on tariff volatility and
 6        supply chain issues. His primary concern appears to be avoiding Route 894 on Links F20
1         and F23, which impact his property.
 8
 9   Q.   DOES MR. HOWTON STATE HE HAS EXPERTISE RELATIVE TO THE
10        ROUTING DECISION INCIDENT TO THESE CCN PROCEEDINGS?
11
12   A.   No. Mr. Howton expressly disclaims expertise in routing, engineering, environmental
13        science, and appraisal.
14
15   Q.   HOW DO YOU RESPOND TO HIS CONCERNS?
16
17   A.   To the extent tariff volatility and supply chain risk is relevant to the analysis, tariff
18        volatility affects all routes similarly as does supply chain risk. These types of"costs" are
19        typically included in the Applicants' contingency costs. Further, supply chain risk is a
20        procurement risk, not a routing criterion.
21
22   Q.   DO YOU CONSIDER MR. HOWTON'S OPINION TO BE A COMPLETE
23        EVALUATION OF ALL RELEVANT CRITERIA SUCH THAT HIS
24        RECOMMENDATIONS SHOULD BE GIVEN THE SAME WEIGHT OR
25        CONSIDERATION AS ONCOR AND LCRA TRANSMISSION SERVICES
26        CORPORATION'S EVALUATION AND RECOMMENDATION OF ROUTE 894
27        AS THE BEST MEETS ROUTE?
28
29   A.   No. In my opinion, the Applicants' evaluation was significantly more comprehensive.
30        Oncor and LCRA, together with their consultants Kimley-Horn and Halff, utilized teams
31        of experienced professionals with expertise in routing, environmental analysis,
32        engineering, constructability, and cost evaluation to perform a broad analysis ofthe routing
33        criteria applicable to this proceeding. Based on my review of that work, I believe they
34        appropriately determined that Route 894 best satisfies the applicable routing criteria.
35
36   Q.   IS IT SURPRISING THAT HIS PRIMARY BASIS FOR RECOMMENDING
37        THESE OTHER ROUTES IS THAT THEY DON'T CROSS HIS PROPERTY?
38
39   A.   No. It is understandable that Mr. Howton would prefer routes that avoid impacts to his
40        property. In my experience, that is a common concern among many i f not most affected
41        landowners and intervenors in transmission routing proceedings.
42
43   Q.   DOES HE RAISE ANY OTHER CONCERNS?
44
45   A.   Yes. Mr. Howton raises several concerns regarding construction, operational, and
46        environmental impacts associated with the proposed transmission line.


                            Rebuttal Testimony ofMark D. Anderson at Page 5
  1
 2   Q.   GIVEN  YOUR            EXPERIENCE  CONSTRUCTING HIGH VOLTAGE
 3        TRANSMISSION          LINES, DO YOU HAVE A RESPONSE TO THESE
 4        CONCERNS?
 5
 6   A.   Yes. In my experience, transmission line owners and construction contractors routinely
1         develop and implement standard pollution prevention, construction, operations, and
 8        maintenance programs for projects of this nature. These programs are typically prepared
 9        by professionals with direct experience in transmission line construction, operation, and
10        maintenance. Once a specific route is approved, those programs are then reviewed and
11        modified as appropriate to address site-specific conditions and environmental
12        considerations associated with the approved route.
13
14   Q.   WHAT DID YOU CONCLUDE FROM YOUR REVIEW OF MR. HOWTON'S
15        TESTIMONY?
16
17   A.   I concluded that Mr. Howton raises legitimate concerns regarding the potential impact of
18        the proposed transmission line on his property and operations. In my opinion, however, the
19        types of concerns he identifies are issues that are commonly evaluated and addressed
20        during the final design, construction, operation, and maintenance phases of transmission
21        line proj ects through prudent engineering practices, site-specific mitigation measures, and
22        established environmental and operational protocols. While affected landowners
23        understandably prefer to avoid these impacts altogether, the presence of such concerns does
24        not, in my opinion, demonstrate that Route 894 fails to satisfy the applicable routing
25        criteria.
26
27
28        B.          RAE LYNN SCHNEIDER REINECKE.
29
30   Q.   HAVE YOU REVIEWED THE TESTIMONY OF RAE LYNN SCHNEIDER
31        REINECKE?
32
33   A.   Yes. Ms. Reinecke evaluated 12 of the 36 environmental criteria identified in the
34        Environmental Assessment and Alternative Route Analysis ("EAARA") and ultimately
35        recommended approval of a relatively new route proposed by intervenor Cherokee Creek
36        Partners, identified in her testimony as Route CCG. She identified 22 reasons supporting
37        her recommendation, even though Route CCG is longer than Route 894, contains more
38        habitable structures within 500 feet, and has a higher estimated cost.
39
40   Q.   WHAT IS YOUR GENERAL IMPRESSION OF HER TESTIMONY?
41
42   A.   In my opinion, she places substantial emphasis on select environmental considerations
43        without fully balancing the broader range of routing factors considered by the Applicants,
44        including overall route length, cost, constructability, and comparative impacts to habitable
45        structures and the surrounding community. By contrast, the Applicants' evaluation



                            Rebuttal Testimony ofMark D. Anderson at Page 6
  1        considered all 36 EAARA criteria together with broader routing and engineering
 2        considerations in determining that Route 894 was the Best Meets route.
 3   Q.   CAN YOU DESCRIBE OR COMPARE HER ROUTE CCG COMPARED TO
 4        JOINT APPLICANTS' BEST MEETS ROUTE 894?
 5
 6   A.   Yes. Route CCG consists of the following links: AO-Al-A2-Bl-821-C4-D12-C5-E52-
 7        Fl-F31-F32-F20-F23-G72-G73-G82-G13-G2-G6-Il-J31-J32-J33-J6-K62-K42-M31-L4-
 8        M22-M23-M5-N4-03-P2-Rl-Tl-T2-Z2.
 9
10        Route 894 consists of the following links: AO-Al-A2-Bl-821-C4-D12-C5-E52-Fl-F31-
11        F32-F20-F23-G72-G73-G82-G13-G51-G52-Hl- H41-H42-J21-J22-J23-J27-J4-Kll-K7-
12        J16-K13-K51-K52-Mll-M12-N3- P2-Ill-Tl-T2-Z2.
13
14        Route CCG is 232.19 miles long, costs $1,754,606,644, and has 105 habitable structures
15        within 500 feet.
16
17        Route 894 is 223.17 miles long, costs $1,680,919,000, and has 85 habitable structures
18        within 500 feet.
19
20   Q.   DID MS. REINECKE MENTION ANY FACTORS RELATED TO COST OR
21        LENGTH COMPARISONS?
22
23   A.   No. She did not include cost or length comparisons. Route CCG is 10.02 miles longer
24        than Route 894 and costs $73,687,000 more than Route 894.
25
26   Q.   CAN YOU EXPLAIN WHY THERE IS SUCH A SIGNIFICANT DIFFERENCE
27        IN LENGTH, COST AND IMPACT BETWEEN ROUTE CCG AND ROUTE 894?
28
29   A.   Yes. In my opinion, the primary reason for the increased length and cost associated with
30        Route CCG is that it departs from the more direct and forward-progressing alignment
31        utilized by Route 894 and instead incorporates a series of directional deviations and
32        meandering link combinations through the central portion of the study area. Although the
33        two routes share many common links at the eastern and western ends of the route, Route
34        CCG diverges from Route 894 at Link G13 and then follows a series of alternating
35        northward and southward movements before reconnecting with Route 894 at Link P2.
36
37        From a routing and constructability perspective, these types of non-forward-progressing
38        link combinations are generally less efficient because they increase overall mileage without
39        producing corresponding forward advancement toward the project endpoints. As a result,
40        they tend to increase total line length, structure count, material quantities, construction
41        duration, landowner impacts, operational complexity, and overall project cost. They also
42        increase the geographic area across which impacts are distributed.
43
44        Specifically, Route CCG proceeds south on Links G2 and G6, then reverses direction and
45        proceeds north on Link Il, continues north on Link J31, turns south again on Link J32,
46        turns north on Link J6, proceeds south on Link K62, turns north again on Link L4, then


                             Rebuttal Testimony ofMark D. Anderson at Page 7
  1        south on Link M22 before ultimately turning north again on Link 03 to reconnect with
 2        Route 894 at Link P2. In my experience, this type of repeated directional shifting reflects
 3        a less direct corridor alignment than Route 894.
 4
 5        By comparison, Route 894 generally maintains a more direct and forward-progressing
 6        alignment through the south-central portion of the study area. That more linear alignment
 7        reduces overall route length and associated construction costs while also reducing the
 8        number of habitable structures affected, the overall footprint of the corridor, and the
 9        number of opportunities for additional environmental, community, and land use conflicts
10        to occur across the study area.
11
12   Q.   DID MS. REINECKE NOTE A DISPARITY IN THE NUMBER OF HABITABLE
13        STRUCTURES BETWEEN ROUTE CCG AND ROUTE 894?
14
15   A.   Yes. Ms. Reinecke acknowledged that Route CCG includes 105 habitable structures within
16        500 feet of the proposed centerline, compared to 85 habitable structures for Route 894. She
17        concluded that the difference of 20 structures fell within approximately one standard
18        deviation of her statistical analysis and therefore considered the two routes comparable for
19        this criterion.
20
21   Q.   GENERALLY, WHAT IS YOUR OPINION REGARDING THE DISPARITY IN
22        HABITABLE STRUCTURES?
23
24   A.   In my opinion, the practical impact of an additional 20 habitable structures is significant
25        from a routing and community-impact perspective. While statistical analysis may be useful
26        as one analytical tool, the Commission must ultimately evaluate the actual impacts to
27        homes, landowners, and communities located along the route. In my experience,
28        minimizing impacts to habitable structures is typically one of the most important routing
29        considerations because those impacts directly affect residents, land use, visual impacts, and
30        overall community compatibility. From that perspective, I consider the difference between
31        85 and 105 habitable structures to be meaningful and not merely a statistically comparable
32        variation.
33
34   Q.   DO YOU CONSIDER MS. REINECKE'S TESTIMONY TO BE A COMPLETE
35        EVALUATION OF ALL RELEVANT CRITERIA SUCH THAT HER
36        RECOMMENDATION SHOULD BE GIVEN THE SAME WEIGHT OR
37        CONSIDERATION  AS    JOINT  APPLICANTS'  EVALUATION   AND
38        RECOMMENDATION FOR ROUTE 894 AS BEST MEETS ROUTE?
39
40   A.   No.
41
42   Q.   DOES IT APPEAR THAT THE PRIMARY BASIS FOR RECOMMENDING
43        THESE OTHER ROUTES IS THAT THEY AVOID IMPACTS TO MS.
44        REINECKE'S CLIENTS' PROPERTIES?
45



                            Rebuttal Testimony ofMark D. Anderson at Page 8
  1   A.   Yes. In my opinion, Route CCG appears designed primarily to shift the route away from
 2        the properties of certain intervenors and landowner groups represented by or aligned with
 3        Cherokee Creek Partners. From a broader routing perspective, shifting impacts from one
 4        group of landowners to multiple other landowners is not necessarily prudent avoidance,
 5        but rather a redistribution of impacts across the study area. It is likely that many other
 6        affected landowners in this proceeding would also prefer that the transmission line not
1         cross their properties.
 8
 9   Q.   WHAT DID YOU CONCLUDE FROM YOUR REVIEW OF MS. REINECKE'S
10        TESTIMONY?
11
12   A.   I concluded that Ms. Reinecke' s testimony was narrower in scope and less comprehensive
13        than the Applicants' evaluation supporting Route 894. In particular, her testimony relied
14        on a partial review of select environmental criteria and a quartile ranking methodology
15        applied to portions of Table 7-2 of the EAARA together with Route CCG data, while
16        placing comparatively less emphasis on broader routing considerations such as overall
17        route length, total proj ect cost, constructability, cumulative community impacts, and the
18        increased number of habitable structures affected by Route CCG. In my opinion, the
19        Applicants' evaluation involved a more robust and balanced consideration of the full range
20        of routing criteria and therefore provides a more reliable basis for concluding that Route
21        894 is the Best Meets route.
22
23
24        C.     MICHAEL D. NOONAN.
25
26   Q.   DID YOU REVIEW THE TESTIMONY OF MICHAEL D. NOONAN?
27
28   A.   Yes. Mr. Noonan testified on behalf of Bar H Bar Ranch and Nature Preserve, which is
29        impacted by Links G52 and Hl. He recommends that those links not be utilized and

32        G6.
33

35
36   A.   Mr. Noonan' s testimony focuses primarily on the localized impacts to the Bar H Bar
37        Ranch property and a limited set of alternative links, rather than a comprehensive
38        corridor-wide evaluation of all route alternatives and criteria applicable to these
39        proceedings.
40
41   Q.   WHAT ARE MR. NOONAN'S STATED REASONS FOR OPPOSING LINKS G52
42        AND Hl?
43
44   A.   Mr. Noonan expresses concerns regarding bifurcation and operational impacts to his
45        property' s hunting and wildlife activities, including the use of aerial herding for exotic
46        species management. He also expresses concern that the transmission line could limit


                            Rebuttal Testimony ofMark D. Anderson at Page 9
  1        future land uses and adversely affect the overall utility and value of the property. Mr.
 2        Noonan also references the potential for significant condemnation-related damages and
 3        costs associated with routing across the property.
 4
 5   Q.   WHAT ARE          YOUR       GENERAL        IMPRESSIONS         REGARDING          THESE
 6        CONCERNS?
1
 8        In my experience, concerns relating to property bifurcation, operational impacts, visual
 9        impacts, and limitations on future land use are not unique to Links G52 and Hl or to the
10        Bar H Bar Ranch property. Those types of impacts are considerations that arise along many
11        potential routes in large transmission proj ects and are therefore appropriately evaluated
12        within a broader corridor-wide balancing analysis, as the Joint Applicants performed in
13        this proceeding. While those concerns are understandable from a landowner perspective,
14        the Commission' s routing analysis focuses primarily on the comparative routing criteria
15        established under PURA and the Commission' s rules, rather than on predicting or
16        comparing future condemnation settlements or litigation outcomes.
17
18
19        D.     JOHN GRIFFIN YATES, JR.
20
21   Q.   DID YOU REVIEW THE TESTIMONY OF JOHN GRIFFIN YATES, JR.?
22
23   A.   Yes. Mr. Yates opposes the use ofLinks J12, J13, J14, J25, J27, and J4 because those links
24        would cross property in which he holds ownership interests in San Saba County. His
25        testimony focuses on the operational, recreational, and long-term land use impacts he

31
32   A.   No. In my experience, those are common concerns raised by landowners involved in major
33        transmission routing proceedings, particularly in rural and ranching areas. Ben E. Keith

35        the operational and land use impacts associated with a transmission corridor crossing their

39

42   A.   Yes. Mr. Yates identifies numerous alternative routes that would avoid his property and
43        specifically references Routes 668, 546, and 551.
44
45   Q.   DOES MR. YATES PROVIDE A ROUTING ANALYSIS IN SUPPORT OF SUCH
46        ROUTES?


                           Rebuttal Testimony of Mark D. Anderson at Page 10
  1
 2        No. His testimony primarily discusses route length and cost. In my opinion, however, route
 3        length and associated cost, while important considerations, are only part of the broader
 4        routing analysis required in a proceeding ofthis nature. Based on my review of the record
 5        in this proceeding, I believe the Joint Applicants performed that broader multi-factor
 6        evaluation when they analyzed the applicable routing criteria and ultimately concluded that
 7        Route 894 is the Best Meets route, to which I concur.
 8

13        Inc., regarding a possible relocation of an existing transmission facility closer to Highway

18   Q.   DO YOU FIND THESE DISCUSSIONS INSTRUCTIVE TO THE ROUTING
19        ISSUES HERE?

22        in this proceeding.

29   A.   Ms. Alexander requests that the Commission reject Route 894 based on the potential

45



                           Rebuttal Testimony of Mark D. Anderson at Page 11
  1   Q.   DO YOU HAVE ANY RESPONSE TO THE TESTIMONY REGARDING
 2        FUTURE DEVELOPMENT PLANS ASSOCIATED WITH SOLANA RANCH?
 3
 4   A.   Yes. Unlike existing land use constraints and established development patterns already
 5        present within the study area, much of Ms. Alexander's testimony regarding Solana Ranch
 6        focuses on future phases of development, anticipated market conditions, and long-term
1         buildout plans that have not yet been fully implemented along Route 894. Consistent with
 8        the Commission' s guidance in Docket No. 57648, future development plans that have not
 9        been initiated in a readily observable or measurable way along the proposed route should
10        not be afforded the same weight as existing routing constraints and established land uses
11        already present in the corridor. While planned future development is an appropriate
12        consideration, in my opinion it should be balanced against the full range of existing
13        environmental, engineering, land use, community, and routing factors evaluated by the
14        Joint Applicants in determining that Route 894 is the Best Meets route.
15
16   Q.   DO YOU AGREE WITH HER CLAIM THAT ROUTE 894 DOES NOT MEET
17        THE COMMISSION'S ROUTING CRITERIA?
18
19   A.   No. I believe as set forth in my Direct Testimony, that Route 894 best meets PURA and
20        the Commission's rules.
21
22
23        F.     AARON BREWER.
24
25   Q.   HAVE YOU REVIEWED THE TESTIMONY OF AARON BREWER?
26
27   A.   Yes. Mr. Brewer testified on behalf of Save the Lampasas, Carpenter Land & Cattle,
28        Martin, and the N3 Opposition Landowner Group. His testimony focuses primarily on
29        opposition to Links G51, G52, J22, J24, and N3, together with his evaluation of route
30        alternatives that would avoid or reduce impacts to those areas. He identifies Route 572 as
31        his preferred route.
32
33   Q.   DO YOU UNDERSTAND WHY MR. BREWER OPPOSES THOSE LINKS?
34
35   A.   Yes. I understand the concerns Mr. Brewer identifies regarding environmental impacts,
36        land fragmentation, visual impacts, and compatibility with existing land uses and natural
37        features. Those are considerations commonly raised in transmission routing proceedings
38        and are among the types of factors evaluated by the Joint Applicants. At the same time,
39        many of those same concerns are present to varying degrees throughout the broader study
40        area and along multiple alternative routes, including routes that would impact Ben E. Keith
41        Company and the Jan Yates Boultinghouse Family Trust properties. In my opinion, the
42        Commission must evaluate those concerns through a broader comparative balancing
43        analysis across all affected routes and landowners rather than focusing primarily on
44        avoiding impacts to any one particular group of links or properties.
45



                           Rebuttal Testimony of Mark D. Anderson at Page 12
  1   Q.   WHAT DO YOU UNDERSTAND THE BASIS OF MR. BREWER' S
 2        RECOMMENDATION OF ROUTE 572 AS HIS BEST MEETS ROUTE TO BE?
